section_summary: This section is dominated by correspondence and detailed enforcement reports concerning Japanese police inspector Shinji Taniguchi’s 1937 visit to the U.S. Pacific Coast to study narcotics control and exchange intelligence on Japanese smuggling networks. The reports discuss the Heian Maru/Tensaka investigation, weaknesses in Japanese distribution controls, proposed stronger Japanese legislation, and arrangements for continuing bilateral cooperation while routing investigations through the Japanese Foreign Office. Later documents transmit the Japanese Government’s 1936 narcotics report and League of Nations corrections, newspaper criticism of Japan’s drug policy, and cross-references concerning opium and heroin traffic in Japanese-controlled areas of China.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Hornbeck letter on narcotics investigations in Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends accepting the Embassy’s procedure for routing American requests for narcotics investigations through Japanese authorities.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck urges encouraging Japanese officials who favor stronger narcotics laws and avoiding antagonism over investigative methods; Tokyo-Kobe telephone contact should suffice if Treasury avoids objectionable police work.

subfiles.title: Notice concerning Shinji Taniguchi’s arrival in the United States
subfiles.about: Reports Taniguchi’s expected Seattle arrival and the waiver of any missing passport visa.
subfiles.summary: State tells Labor that Shinji Taniguchi would reach Seattle September 21 to study narcotics control; visa requirement waived if necessary and Seattle immigration alerted.

subfiles.title: Subject jacket for Traffic in Narcotics—Japan
subfiles.about: Identifies the case jacket for State Department records on narcotics traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Subject jacket for Traffic in Narcotics—Japan with file and case numbers.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch transmitting Japan’s 1936 narcotics report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of the Japanese Government’s official report on narcotics traffic for 1936.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards two English copies of Japan's annual 1936 report on opium and dangerous drugs from the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japan’s 1936 narcotics report to the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy despatch and Japanese annual report and requests Treasury comments.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury the Embassy despatch and Japan's 1936 narcotics report, inviting comments.

subfiles.title: Labor Department report on Taniguchi’s admission at Seattle
subfiles.from: I. F. Wixon, Immigration and Naturalization Service
subfiles.about: Confirms that Taniguchi arrived at Seattle and was admitted on primary inspection with a Section 3(1) visa.
subfiles.summary: Immigration and Naturalization Service reports Taniguchi arrived at Seattle September 21 with the required visa.

subfiles.title: Treasury letter transmitting Anslinger’s report on Taniguchi
subfiles.from: Wayne C. Taylor for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Transmits Anslinger’s conference report and asks State to express appreciation to Japan and encourage Taniguchi’s retention in narcotics work.
subfiles.summary: Treasury sees Taniguchi's visit as evidence of Japanese interest in suppressing narcotics traffic and asks Fuller to use informal League contacts to support his continuation.

subfiles.title: Anslinger memorandum on conferences with Shinji Taniguchi
subfiles.about: Reports discussions with Taniguchi on smuggling cases, Japanese control weaknesses, addiction, legislation, and future cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger describes Taniguchi’s assignment following the Heian Maru seizure and reviews Japanese arrests, suspected traffickers, pharmaceutical sources, Dairen and Tientsin smuggling, and cases involving morphine and cocaine. The conference concluded that diversion chiefly occurred after drugs left factories because wholesalers and retailers were inadequately controlled. Taniguchi discussed a central narcotics bureau and legislation increasing penalties, while Anslinger recommended expressing appreciation, supporting Taniguchi’s continued assignment, and arranging recurring exchanges between American and Japanese enforcement officers.

subfiles.title: Telegram instructing Tokyo to express appreciation for Taniguchi’s visit
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to thank Japanese authorities for Taniguchi’s visit and confidentially convey the hope that he remains in narcotics work.
subfiles.summary: The telegram summarizes Taniguchi’s meetings at Seattle and San Francisco and his duties concerning the Heian Maru case, police coordination, and Home Office cooperation. The Embassy is instructed to express American appreciation and report that enforcement officials believe the visit improved mutual understanding.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning reports on Taniguchi
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Treasury’s report and requests copies of Customs reports on Taniguchi’s conferences.
subfiles.summary: State advises Treasury that Anslinger’s report is being transmitted to the Embassy in Tokyo. It also describes the telegram thanking Japan, noting improved mutual understanding, and conveying Treasury’s wish that Taniguchi continue his narcotics assignment.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal of Seattle Customs reports
subfiles.about: Transmits reports by Seattle Customs officers concerning their conferences with Taniguchi.
subfiles.summary: Treasury forwards two Seattle Customs reports (October 4 and 13, 1937) on Taniguchi's meetings with Customs officials.

subfiles.title: Bradt and Atherton report on Taniguchi’s Seattle visit
subfiles.from: Fred H. Bradt and A. S. Atherton, forwarded by Joseph L. Green
subfiles.about: Details Taniguchi’s Seattle conferences, inspection visits, interview with Tensaka, and information about suspected smugglers.
subfiles.summary: The report covers Taniguchi’s arrival, discussions of Japanese narcotics controls, and a list of earlier seizures from Japanese vessels. It describes his visit to the Seattle Police Department and McNeil Island Penitentiary, where he interviewed Soiichi Tensaka. Information obtained from Tensaka and Yamamoto implicated Watanabe and others in financing or transporting narcotics between Japan and the United States, leading to further meetings in Los Angeles.

subfiles.title: Hanks report on Taniguchi’s Pacific Coast conferences
subfiles.about: Reports Taniguchi’s San Francisco conference, findings from the Nonaka–Tensaka investigation, and official tours arranged during his visit.
subfiles.summary: Hanks recounts Taniguchi’s explanation of the Heian Maru investigation, Japanese distribution controls, weak penalties, proposed reforms, and arrests in Osaka and Dairen. Participants favored keeping Taniguchi in his post and establishing regular reciprocal visits by American and Japanese officers. The report also records tours of police departments, prisons, a film studio, and other sites in Los Angeles and San Francisco before Taniguchi sailed home aboard the Taiyo Maru.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction forwarding Taniguchi conference reports
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential reports and letters concerning Taniguchi’s conferences with Treasury officials.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends the Tokyo Embassy reports by Anslinger, Bradt and Atherton, and Hanks. It also encloses personal letters to Masayuki Yokoyama and Shiko Kusama intended to encourage support for Taniguchi’s work.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting “More Drugs for China”
subfiles.about: Sends the Embassy a photostatic copy of a New Statesman and Nation article about drugs in China.
subfiles.summary: Department sends the Tokyo Embassy the article More Drugs for China (October 9, 1937) for information.

subfiles.title: Notification to Treasury of reports sent to Tokyo
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Informs Treasury that the Customs and Narcotics reports on Taniguchi were forwarded to the Tokyo Embassy.
subfiles.summary: State believes the reports will assist the Embassy in handling cooperation on narcotics matters. It also reports that personal letters are being sent to Masayuki Yokoyama and Shiko Kusama.

subfiles.title: Personal letter to Shiko Kusama about Taniguchi
subfiles.about: Describes the favorable American impression of Taniguchi and suggests that his continued narcotics assignment would benefit both countries.
subfiles.summary: Fuller recounts Taniguchi’s Pacific Coast conferences and the appreciation expressed by American authorities. He emphasizes Taniguchi’s careful study of legislative reform, sincerity, and initiative, implicitly inviting Kusama’s support for keeping him in the work.

subfiles.title: Personal letter to Masayuki Yokoyama about Taniguchi
subfiles.about: Reports the success of Taniguchi’s visit and argues that retaining him would serve mutual American and Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Fuller describes Taniguchi’s conferences with Customs and Narcotics officers and the improved understanding they produced. He highlights Taniguchi’s study of legislative reform, sincerity, and initiative, and closes with greetings to Yokoyama and his wife.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch on official Japanese thanks for Taniguchi’s reception
subfiles.about: Reports the exchange of diplomatic notes thanking Japan for Taniguchi’s visit and the United States for assisting him.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Embassy thanked the Foreign Office October 28 and the Foreign Minister replied November 4 thanking for Taniguchi's treatment.

subfiles.title: Grew note to Foreign Minister Hirota
subfiles.about: Expresses American appreciation for Japan’s dispatch of Taniguchi to investigate narcotics smuggling.
subfiles.summary: Grew tells Foreign Minister Hirota that American authorities were pleased with Taniguchi's visit, which improved mutual understanding on suppressing narcotics traffic.

subfiles.title: Hirota reply concerning Taniguchi’s American visit
subfiles.about: Thanks American authorities for assisting Taniguchi and promises continued cooperation against Pacific narcotics smuggling.
subfiles.summary: Hirota reports Taniguchi returned October 24 praising American kindness, and says Japan will keep close relations with the U.S. on narcotics smuggling.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch on Japanese invitation to American narcotics officers
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese invitation for American narcotics officials, or the Kobe Treasury representative, to conduct a reciprocal visit in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office delivered Mitani’s letter to Anslinger and said Japanese officials would welcome American officers visiting in the same capacity as Taniguchi. It alternatively offered facilities to Treasury representative Scott at Kobe, while cautioning that narcotics matters would continue to pass through the Embassy and Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Mitani letter inviting American narcotics officials to Japan
subfiles.about: Thanks the Bureau of Narcotics for its treatment of Taniguchi and offers facilities for future American official visits to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mitani relays Taniguchi's appreciation, argues reciprocal knowledge improves cooperation, and promises to welcome American narcotics officials studying Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of “Japan and the Drug Trade” clipping
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of a New Statesman and Nation clipping criticizing Japan’s role in the drug trade.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury two photostats of the October 23, 1937 clipping Japan and the Drug Trade.

subfiles.title: “Japan and the Drug Trade”
subfiles.to: Editor and readers of the New Statesman and Nation
subfiles.about: Accuses Japanese authorities and industry of facilitating narcotics production and distribution in Japan, Korea, Manchukuo, and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Young's letter claims Japanese denials delayed action against drug trafficking and alleges opium cultivation, poppy refuse sales, concealed Kobe imports and expansion in China fed distribution.

subfiles.title: Title page of the Japanese Government’s annual narcotics report for 1936
subfiles.about: Identifies Japan’s annual report on opium and other dangerous drugs for 1936.
subfiles.summary: Title page of Japan's 1936 annual narcotics report, communicated under the Narcotics Limitation Convention.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the League copy of Japan’s 1936 report
subfiles.about: Forwards Japan’s 1936 annual narcotics report and additional copies for relevant American agencies.
subfiles.summary: State transmits the League copy of Japan's 1936 report under the 1931 Convention, with copies for the Commissioner of Narcotics, Public Health Service and Customs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to League minutes on the Far Eastern narcotics situation
subfiles.about: Points to another file containing a League circular and minutes on narcotics conditions in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to League circular C.L. 203 (December 1) with an extract of Opium Advisory Committee minutes on the Far Eastern narcotics situation.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment of Japan’s 1936 annual report
subfiles.from: Administrative Assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Japan’s 1936 report on opium and other dangerous drugs.
subfiles.summary: Treasury confirms receipt of the State Department’s December 10 communication and the enclosed Japanese annual report. The text notes the report’s submission under the 1931 Narcotics Limitation Convention and its transmission by the League of Nations; page 378 is a duplicate copy.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the first erratum to Japan’s 1936 annual report
subfiles.about: Forwards duplicate copies of a League of Nations correction to Japan’s 1936 narcotics report.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury the January 1938 erratum correcting Japan's 1936 annual report.

subfiles.title: League of Nations erratum correcting “Manchukuo” to “China”
subfiles.to: Council and members of the League
subfiles.about: Corrects a geographical error in the Japanese Government’s 1936 narcotics report.
subfiles.summary: League erratum: in Annex B on Foreign Office Ordinance No. 11, Manchukuo on page 13 should read China.

subfiles.title: League publication front matter for Japan’s 1936 narcotics report
subfiles.from: Japanese Government and League of Nations Secretary-General
subfiles.to: Parties to the 1931 Convention and other states
subfiles.about: Lists the territorial sections of Japan’s annual report on opium and dangerous drugs for 1936.
subfiles.summary: League front matter for Japan's 1936 narcotics report, covering Japan proper, Korea, Taiwan, Kwantung and the mandated islands, with special reports on prepared opium and the Hankow and Tientsin concessions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning Shiko Kusama’s planned Washington visit
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch concerning Kusama’s plan to travel via Washington for meetings with Fuller and Anslinger.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Opium Board member Shiko Kusama planned to leave for Geneva March 9 and wished to confer in Washington with Fuller and Anslinger.

subfiles.title: Request for a 1924 League document on suppressing heroin manufacture
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in charge, Geneva
subfiles.about: Requests two copies of a League document containing a Japanese statement on suppressing heroin manufacture.
subfiles.summary: Geneva consular officer is asked to obtain League document O.C. 210 of June 4, 1924, a Japanese letter on suppressing heroin manufacture.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to arrests and heroin seizures in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram requesting information about arrests and a large heroin seizure reported in the press.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a report on the arrest of seven Japanese and Manchurians and seizure of seven truckloads of heroin, requested after a March 14 Daily Telegraph article.

subfiles.title: Treasury coordinator’s reply on investigative procedure in Japan
subfiles.about: Confirms Treasury’s acceptance of the procedure requiring narcotics-investigation requests in Japan to pass through the Embassy and Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The coordinator explains why Hornbeck’s September 1937 letter had not initially received a reply and notes the change from Harold Graves to a new coordinator. Treasury accepts the procedure used since 1933, although it regrets the limited progress achieved and the failure of Geneva representations to improve matters.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Embassy despatch on Japanese thanks
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of Grew’s despatch and enclosures documenting the exchange of thanks over Taniguchi’s visit.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury despatch No. 2656 (November 9, 1937) and notes, completing Treasury's record of Taniguchi's visit.

subfiles.title: Personal letter to Grew on investigative procedure and narcotics cooperation
subfiles.about: Confirms approval of Grew’s procedure for narcotics cases and reviews recent Japanese-American cooperation and personnel visits.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck tells Grew Treasury accepted the Embassy-Foreign Office channel, praises the Taniguchi and Kusama visits, names Irey as Treasury coordinator, and notes no narcotics seized from Japanese ships since the Heian Maru case.

subfiles.title: Request that Anslinger acknowledge Mitani’s invitation
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Suggests that Anslinger thank Mitani for offering facilities to visiting American narcotics officials.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury a duplicate copy of Mitani’s November 8 letter concerning Taniguchi’s visit. It proposes that Anslinger acknowledge the invitation, say the government will keep it in mind, and return his reply for transmission through diplomatic channels.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Grew concerning a possible Anslinger reply
subfiles.about: Advises the Embassy that Mitani’s letter was sent to Treasury and leaves delivery of any reply to Embassy discretion.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Grew that Treasury was invited to prepare an Anslinger reply to Japan's willingness to receive American narcotics officials, delivery at the Embassy's discretion.

subfiles.title: Telegram approving centralized narcotics-information procedure in Japan
subfiles.about: Approves Grew’s procedure for routing narcotics intelligence through the Japanese Foreign Office and confirms Treasury’s agreement.
subfiles.summary: The Department recognizes Japan’s objection to independent American police investigations and direct local exchanges with consular or Treasury representatives. Because American activity in Japanese territory requires Japanese assent, it approves the Embassy–Foreign Office channel. It nevertheless hopes telephone and telegraph use can reduce delays for the Treasury representative at Kobe.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on proposed Japanese opium monopolies in China
subfiles.about: Points to information about proposed Japanese-controlled opium monopolies in North and Central China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japan contemplated opium monopolies in North China under the North China Army and in Central China under the Shanghai Army.

subfiles.title: League of Nations second erratum to Japan’s 1936 narcotics report
subfiles.to: Council and members of the League
subfiles.about: Corrects the number of licensed prepared-opium retail shops in Taiwan in Japan’s 1936 report.
subfiles.summary: League second erratum: in Table VI on Taiwan, licensed retail shops on December 31, 1936 should read 331, not none.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the second erratum to Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards duplicate copies of the second League correction to Japan’s 1936 narcotics report.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury the League's April 7 second erratum in duplicate for its records.
